Lessons.Title: Represent Data in Scaled Bar Graphs
ExplanationParagraphs: Grade 3 Unit 1 Lesson 5, 2021 first edition of Illustrative Mathematics K–5, teaches students to represent categorical data using a scaled BAR graph and connect a one-unit number scale to scales of two or five. This is a source-semantic first-party teaching body, not the original publisher's exact image or paper layout.

Warm-up — Number Talk: Twos and Fives (10 minutes). Original four expressions are 2+2+2+2 = 8; 2+2+2+2+2+2+2+2 = 16; 5+5+5+5 = 20; and 5+5+5+5+5+5+5+5 = 40. Take one minute silent thinking, then discuss mental strategies, especially doubling the number of equal addends to double the result.

Activity 1 — Compare Bar Graphs (10 minutes). The original How We Get Home categories and exact totals are Bike 12, Walk 4, Bus or Van 6, Car 3. A one-unit bar graph and a two-unit scaled bar graph represent IDENTICAL quantities, even if their tick spacing and plotted heights look different. Graphs start at zero and have category labels outside the plot area. Students compare similarities and differences with a partner (one minute silent and four minutes partner), and teachers judge reasoning, not merely four supplementary numeric questions.

Activity 2 — Create a Scaled Bar Graph (25 minutes). Reuse the actual class-preference survey collected in Lesson 4, not the fixed travel-home example. Each pupil should bring their earlier picture graph and choose a vertical-axis tick spacing of TWO or FIVE, with a title and the six teacher-collected original categories Car, Train, Boat, Balloon, Plane, Helicopter. The source supplies a blank scale-by-two graph to 16 or a scale-by-five graph to 40. Choose a sensible scaling and accurately position a bar whose count falls between ticks, including odds and nonmultiples of five; NEVER round a real respondent away. Partner construction is approximately 12 minutes. Compare the graphs built with the two scales, justify the choice with the teacher and optionally draw both. MLR7 and chunked support are teacher-led.

Lesson synthesis (10 minutes) BEFORE the five-minute Cool-down: teach a friend that the interval between ticks represents 2 or 5, and that choosing the scale requires checking the class values. Original publisher Teacher Guide Cool-down Complete a Scaled Bar Graph is a zoo preference survey: Elephant 17, Tiger 10, Giraffe 14 and Otter 4. A child completes the missing TIGER=10 and OTTER=4 bars in a newly authored graph with original 5-unit tick scale and exact intermediate positions; the teacher must inspect actual bar-drawing work. Independent Edulytics club questions are optional extra practice, not the publisher source task. AFTER the Cool-down, Math Community spends 2–3 minutes revising classroom norms, which require live teacher review.

KeyConcepts.Title: One-unit versus scaled bar axes
KeyConcepts.Definition: A scaled bar graph uses ticks separated by more than one number; the original category totals are unchanged.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Compare named quantities, not only visual bar height; category counts are identical in the two original How We Get Home graphs.
KeyConcepts.Example: Bike = 12 in both scales, Walk = 4, Bus or Van = 6 and Car = 3.

KeyConcepts.Title: Exact data from the previous lesson
KeyConcepts.Definition: Lesson 5 depends on the real travel-preference survey that pupils gathered in Lesson 4.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Re-use teacher-authenticated real category values; do not import the fixed four-category How We Get Home counts in place of the six actual class categories.
KeyConcepts.Example: Car, Train, Boat, Balloon, Plane and Helicopter counts differ by classroom; teacher checks the actual prior graph.

KeyConcepts.Title: Choose scale of two or five
KeyConcepts.Definition: The choice of axis tick spacing changes how data are represented, not the recorded values.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Place every bar at its actual value even if between marked ticks. Scale by 2 or 5 and start at zero; do not round counts to multiples of the scale.
KeyConcepts.Example: Nine pupils on an axis by five must be plotted at 9, between 5 and 10, not at 5 or 10.

KeyConcepts.Title: Bar-graph source Cool-down
KeyConcepts.Definition: The published teacher-guide Cool-down checks whether a pupil can complete a scaled bar graph from a four-category zoo table.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Teacher checks all category labels and that missing Tiger and Otter bars reach exactly 10 and 4, respectively.
KeyConcepts.Example: The table gives Elephant 17, Tiger 10, Giraffe 14, Otter 4.

WorkedExamples.Title: Source number talk: twice as many equal groups
WorkedExamples.Question: Find four groups of two, eight groups of two, four groups of five and eight groups of five mentally.
WorkedExamples.Method: Skip-count and double the earlier sum rather than separately adding every term.
Steps: Doubling the four twos gives eight twos: 8 + 8 = 16.

WorkedExamples.Title: Activity 1 source bars: the same four counts
WorkedExamples.Question: Bike 12, Walk 4, Bus or Van 6, Car 3 are shown with axes by one and by two. Did the student population change?
WorkedExamples.Method: Read the named count of each category from both graph keys.
Steps: Verify both graphs start at zero.
On the by-two axis match bar heights to exactly those same numbers, even when Car 3 lies between 2 and 4.
Add 12 + 4 + 6 + 3 to find the same sample size.
WorkedExamples.Answer: The two graphs show the same 25 learners.

WorkedExamples.Title: Activity 2 accurate class-specific chart
WorkedExamples.Question: A fictional teacher-approved class dataset contains Car 3, Train 6, Boat 1, Balloon 5, Plane 4, Helicopter 2. Where should Car and Balloon stop with a by-two axis?
WorkedExamples.Method: Illustrative data only; actual class survey must come from pupils' Lesson 4 sheet.
Steps: Start every bar at zero and label all six travel categories.
Mark the vertical axis at 0,2,4,6 and so on.
Draw Car to exactly 3, between 2 and 4; draw Balloon to exactly 5, between 4 and 6.
Check the names and true values on the source teacher's actual sheet, rather than replacing those class values with the fictional sample.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Car reaches 3 and Balloon reaches 5, with no rounding.
WorkedExamples.Check: Both bars land halfway between adjacent by-two marks: 2<3<4 and 4<5<6.

WorkedExamples.Title: Original 2021 source Cool-down: zoo preference table
WorkedExamples.Question: A zoo survey lists Elephant 17, Tiger 10, Giraffe 14, Otter 4. Complete the missing Tiger and Otter bars.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use a single consistent axis tick scale and check that the bar reaches the precise student count. Teacher reviews actual graph geometry.
Steps: Mark a zero-aligned vertical axis with ticks 0,5,10,15,20; Elephant 17 falls between 15 and 20, and Giraffe 14 between 10 and 15.
For the missing Tiger category plot exactly 10 students.
For the missing Otter category plot exactly 4 students.
Verify all bars start at zero, preserve category labels, and check the pupil's drawing with the teacher.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Tiger bar = 10 students; Otter bar = 4 students.
WorkedExamples.Check: The original teacher guide specifically identifies the Tiger 10 and Otter 4 bars as required completions.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Using the previous lesson's real survey categories as if they were the fixed four-category How We Get Home graph.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Activity 1 has four fixed categories while Activity 2 depends on six genuine student-chosen ways of travel collected in Lesson 4.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use the original numbers 12/4/6/3 for Activity 1, and independently approved class totals for Activity 2.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Rounding a bar with a nonmultiple of 2 or 5 to its nearest tick.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The graph's numeric tick interval is not a constraint requiring categorical counts to be multiples of the step.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Draw the bar endpoint between labelled ticks, with its actual height such as 3, 9 or 17.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Mixing up scaled bar graph axis increments with value labels.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Changing scale does not multiply or divide the underlying categorical survey count.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Label the vertical axis 0,2,4 or 0,5,10 and measure each bar's actual quantity without changing raw values.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating an independently authored Science/Art/Music Cool-down as the original zoo source task.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The 2021 Teacher Guide's original five-minute Cool-down requires completing the Tiger and Otter bars from 17/10/14/4 Zoo animal data.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Present the newly authored source-aligned zoo task as the five-minute Cool-down and keep all independent club checks optional.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating the original zoo Cool-down as a unit-one bar graph or rounding Elephant 17, Giraffe 14, Otter 4 to nearest five.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Original 2021 teaching guide expects scaled five-unit tick labels and exact bar heights; its remediation highlights using a scale of one instead of five as an error.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Mark 0,5,10,15,20 and set heights to 17,10,14,4; teacher checks drawn ends between ticks.

SummaryPoints: 2021 Number Talk: four 2s=8; eight 2s=16; four 5s=20; eight 5s=40, with mental doubling and spoken partner strategies.
2021 Activity 1: same original How We Get Home category counts Bike 12, Walk 4, Bus or Van 6, Car 3 under one-unit and two-unit vertical axes; partner comparisons teacher-reviewed.
2021 Activity 2: actual six-category pupil survey from Lesson 4, choose and explain a 2-unit or 5-unit bar graph, exact values between ticks, axes from zero and labelled category names.
10-minute synthesis before five-minute original-source-aligned Cool-down. Source 2021 zoo table Elephant17 Tiger10 Giraffe14 Otter4, with Tiger10 and Otter4 bars completed under human graph review.
Math Community group norms reviewed for 2–3 minutes AFTER Cool-down. Publisher art un-reused; source's instructional mathematics authored independently, with tests written but not executed.

2021 optional centers: Sort and Display Stage 3 Scaled Graphs, and Five in a Row: Addition and Subtraction Stage 6 within 100 with composing; teacher-led, not falsely counted as graded source responses.
